title: Schools White Paper: What’s realistic, what’s missing and what matters most
label: 15 September 2026 · White Paper evidence
summary: MPs questioned education leaders about the Government’s Schools White Paper, covering how to avoid overloading schools with reforms, the role of technical education and local place-based planning, trust governance and parent engagement, admissions and falling pupil numbers, enrichment and attendance, and what should be prioritised. The witnesses urged clearer sequencing, more funding, stronger local partnerships, better support for inclusion and belonging, and fewer, clearer national asks so schools can focus on the things that make the most difference.

chapters.title: Too much change, too fast
chapters.takeaway: Schools face a long list of new asks; ministers should sequence reforms, fund them, and focus on a few game-changing priorities.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: There’s a lot in the Schools White Paper — 100-plus commitments were mentioned. How do we avoid overburdening schools and keep the most important things?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: The sheer number is a problem. We need clear sequencing, strong implementation plans and extra money — otherwise schools will be stretched too thin.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Local councils can help deliver some things, but flexibility is vital. Councils and schools know their communities and should be allowed to implement reforms at sensible speeds.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: The White Paper asks too much at once. Ministers should pick a few ‘game changers’ — e.g., fixing the GCSE issue for the lowest third, improving transition from primary to secondary, and valuing vocational routes — rather than piling on tasks.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: If belonging and engagement are really core aims, they should be embedded in daily school practice, not treated as yet another add-on that increases workload.

chapters.title: Technical education and local jobs
chapters.takeaway: Improving technical qualifications at 16 is right, but they must be rigorous, not lock young people in by place, and link to real local job opportunities.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: The Government wants new technical routes; will schools be able to deliver them, especially in rural areas with few employers or colleges?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: They’re deliverable but need local planning. Rural areas face bigger hurdles for placements, travel and available teachers. The routes must connect to jobs.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: There’s a real problem: many technical awards at 16 aren’t nationally rigorous. The solution is to raise their standards, align them with further/ higher technical qualifications, and work with local employers.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: Should young people be kept broad until 16 so they don’t get locked into local, narrow routes?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Yes. Don’t use the word ‘pathway’ in a way that locks children in. Keep options open so pupils can switch between technical and academic learning.

chapters.title: Trusts, governance and parents
chapters.takeaway: Multi-academy trusts can improve struggling schools, but parents often feel disconnected and accountability and local governance need to be clearer and more visible.

turns.speaker: Jess Asato
turns.text: The White Paper pushes more schools into trusts. Evidence on trusts improving outcomes is mixed. What about staff pay and transparency?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Our research shows real long-term improvement in many formerly struggling schools after joining strong trusts — especially in deprived areas. But results vary and we’re not claiming a simple causal link.

turns.speaker: Jess Asato
turns.text: Parents tell MPs they can’t find anyone to complain to after they’ve raised an issue with a school in a trust. That sense of disconnection is real.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: I didn’t mean to blame parents. Trusts are legally required to publish trustees and governance details; the issue is ensuring strong local governance so parents have a visible route to raise concerns.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Parents in my area also say they feel more disconnected after schools join trusts. Inspection of whole trusts — rather than just schools — might improve transparency and public trust.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Governance can be a local anchor. But some trusts lack local governance people can join. If we want schools rooted in place, local governing bodies must have real agency, or volunteers will walk away.

chapters.title: Admissions, falling rolls and local powers
chapters.takeaway: Falling pupil numbers and schools that move out of local planning make strategic place-based school planning hard; councils need stronger backstop powers and clearer admission rules.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: The White Paper suggests changes to admissions and fair access. What’s the right balance between local authorities and schools/trusts?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Local authorities must be able to place children quickly. There should be better powers when schools resist admitting pupils — especially mid-year — so no child stays without a place.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But academies can leave local place-planning when they convert, which can undermine area-wide planning. Do councils need more powers?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Yes. Authorities need backstop powers to ensure the right places exist across their areas, irrespective of maintained or academy status. That’s crucial with falling birth rates.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: With shrinking rolls, what are the options for keeping small rural schools open?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Work in partnership: federations, shared provision, adding SEND hubs, early years or alternative provision on site — don’t close schools unless you’ve exhausted these options.

chapters.title: Enrichment, attendance and behaviour — belonging matters
chapters.takeaway: Enrichment, belonging and good relationships improve attendance and behaviour, but schools need funding, transport solutions and time; punitive fines and rigid behaviour rules aren’t the answer.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: How do we make enrichment—art, music, after-school activities—available to every child, including rural and special schools?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Funding and transport are the blockers. Councils can support enrichment using libraries, leisure centres and the HAF scheme — the Holiday Activities and Food programme — but need more cash to expand it.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Enrichment builds joy, belonging and skills, but schools are squeezed. Whitehall shouldn’t micromanage what enrichment looks like in each place; it should fund it and let local partners deliver.

turns.speaker: Mrs Brackenridge
turns.text: Attendance is still poor for many pupils. The White Paper wants support first before penalties. Is that right?

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Yes. Work out why children aren’t attending — health, fear, family issues — and fix those root causes. Fines hit the poorest families hardest and often don’t work.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: We have a social contract issue post‑covid: some parents feel school is optional. Rebuilding trust and relationships between schools, parents and pupils is key to improving attendance and behaviour.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: What about behaviour policies like silent corridors or rigid rules?

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Some harsh practices do more harm than good. Teachers need training on relational approaches, trauma awareness and inclusion, and they need time to build those relationships.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Initial teacher training should include more on recognising early trauma and on relational approaches — that helps all pupils, not just those with difficulties.

chapters.title: Accountability, assessment and priorities
chapters.takeaway: Measures like Progress 8 and PISA can’t be the only focus; ministers should simplify, fund, and back schools for multi-year culture change while prioritising a few clear reforms.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: The White Paper suggests tweaks to Progress 8 (the school performance measure covering progress in specific GCSE subjects). Should it change?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Progress 8 has useful elements, especially the breadth it enshrines, but changing metrics is complex. We need to see precise proposals before backing changes.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: What should ministers learn from the international PISA tests — that compare countries on reading, maths and science?

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: PISA is an imperfect international snapshot and can be over-used politically. It’s better to focus on making schools welcoming and on fixing domestic problems such as literacy and the gap for the lowest-performing third.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: PISA stories get spun different ways. Meanwhile, a third of pupils score low at GCSE English — that’s a domestic disgrace. Give those young people qualifications with dignity so they can go forward.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Ministers should listen to the sector on what ‘place’ policy really means, be clear about what local governance should be, and avoid turning new expectations into more sticks that push schools away from collaboration.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If ministers can take only a few actions from our witnesses’ advice, what should they prioritise?

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Back long-term culture change: support schools in a way that isn’t punitive while they embed relational and belonging practices — it takes time.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: Cut the list: pick real game-changers, fund them, and trust headteachers to focus on those rather than 104 new initiatives.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Build genuinely local governance with real agency, and define clearly what a community anchor school should be — and listen to pupils, parents and volunteers in those places.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you — your message is clear: fewer, better-supported reforms, more funding especially for inclusion and enrichment, stronger local partnerships, and measures that back schools to improve rather than punish them.
